desc:
A hall has capacity seats. Each booking is [start, end, seats]: it reserves seats seats for the half-open time range [start, end). Bookings are made one after another and the hall never rejects them.

Return the 0-based index of the first booking after which there is some moment at which the total reserved seats exceed capacity. If this never happens, return -1.

bookings = [[1, 5, 3], [3, 8, 2], [4, 6, 2]], capacity = 6  ->  2
bookings = [[1, 5, 3], [5, 9, 3]],            capacity = 3  -> -1

In the first example, at time 4 the first three bookings together reserve 3 + 2 + 2 = 7 seats; the first two alone reserve at most 5.
constraints: bookings[i] = [start, end, seats] with 0 ≤ start < end ≤ 10<sup>9</sup> and 1 ≤ seats ≤ 10,000
hints: Re-checking the hall after every single booking costs O(n) or O(n log n) each time. Is there something monotonic you can search over?
If the first k bookings already overflow the hall, then so do the first k + 1 bookings (more reservations never help). So the answer is the smallest k where the prefix overflows.

Binary search on the prefix length. To test a prefix, sweep its events: +seats at start, -seats at end, sorted by time with the negative changes first at equal times, and see if the running total ever exceeds capacity.
editorial: Define overflow(k) as: do the first k bookings together exceed the capacity at some moment? Adding bookings can only increase the load at every moment, so overflow is monotone: false, false, ..., true, true. The answer is the (0-based) index of the first booking for which it becomes true.

Evaluating overflow(k) is a plain sweep: build the events (start, +seats) and (end, -seats), sort them (a pair with a negative change sorts before a positive one at the same time, so a booking that ends at t frees its seats before a booking starting at t takes seats), and track the running total. With binary search over k the total cost is O(n log2 n) time and O(n) space.
Check the full list first: if even all bookings fit, the answer is -1.
